To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the architecture of language‐related networks differs between men and women, and between right‐ and left‐hander.

(a) the left‐hemispheric language network is stronger in right‐handed than in left‐handed subjects and stronger in men than in left‐handers and women; (b) the homologue of the left‐hemisperic network in the right hemisphere is weak in right‐hander men; (c) the right‐hemispheric network is equally well developed in left‐hander men and women;

right‐hander males show a left lateralized language organization with a massive interconnectivity of the left‐hemispheric language areas, whereas women and left‐handers show a more bilateral and less interhemispheric language organization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural basis of language processing in healthy individuals.
understanding how language networks are organized in the human brain, and how they are shaped by genetic and experiential factors.
the functional and structural organization of the human language system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human brain is a sexually dimorphic organ, and that the sex difference is not only in size but also in structure, function, and connectivity.

right‐hander males have more connections in the left‐hemispheric language network than females and left‐hander males, and that right‐handers have more left‐hemispherically oriented connections than left‐handers.
language networks in right‐handed males are strongly lateralized to the left hemisphere with a high degree of interconnectivity between the language areas in that hemisphere.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in men the brain networks for language processing are strongly lateralized, whereas in women they are more bilateral.
the language system is organized differently in women and left‐hander men.
the architecture of language areas in the brain is different in right‐handed and left‐handered subjects and in men and women.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the architecture of language processing networks is shaped by sex and hand preference.
the brain is a complex network and that the network is shaped by the interaction between the genes and the environment.

there are sex and handedness differences in the architecture of language‐processing networks in the brain, and that these differences are related to differences in the density of interhemisphere connections between language‐processing areas.
